entries.keyArgument:
A married woman writes anonymously to complain that her parents' generation is pressing her to have children she does not want, and that the pressure is common enough among young couples to amount to a national problem. American mothers, she notes, have stopped worrying that their unmarried daughters will have babies and begun worrying that their married daughters will not.

What makes the piece remarkable is that every argument now treated as contemporary is already fully formed: children are no longer economic assets as they were for her farming great-grandparents; a child would cost her job and a third of the household income in a three-room New York apartment; she has no religious compunction and does not think marriage without children immoral; patriotic pronatalism leaves her cold, with France paying bonuses and Mussolini holding contests for big families; and she refuses the premise that propagation should be the aim of life, having married for love and for the fun of living together.

A 1933 voice making the freedom-and-fulfilment case that survey research would begin measuring ninety years later.
entries.sourceFile: Must I have Children 1933 (scan + transcription + Internet Archive source page)
entries.title: Must I Have Children?

entries.keyArgument:
Davis reads the falling birth rate as the end point of a long institutional devolution rather than as a change in individual motives. From the medieval towns onward, as labour specialised, technology elaborated and social mobility quickened, the reproductive institutions that had held fertility high loosened, shrank and lost their functions.

He insists that stopping the explanation at birth control is inadequate, since contraception is an instrument and not a cause, and that listing motives for using it merely restates the question. The deliberate pronatalist efforts of modern states are, on this reading, the latest result of the same trend, and they may be completing the decline of the old procreative institutions while foreshadowing new ones.
entries.title: Reproductive Institutions and the Pressure for Population

entries.citationNote: Not in your corpus. Added from the published literature; page range should be confirmed against the volume.
entries.keyArgument:
The canonical statement of demographic transition theory, and the text against which Davis 1945 is usually read. Notestein sets out the three-stage scheme of high growth potential, transitional growth and incipient decline, and projects it forward onto the world's regions.

His causal account locates the fertility decline in urban industrial society's dissolution of the family as a productive unit, alongside rising individualism and the growing cost of children. Everything later theorists argue about, including wealth flows, institutions and ideation, is a response to the mechanism proposed here.
entries.title: Population: The Long View
entries.venue: Food for the World (ed. Theodore W. Schultz)

entries.keyArgument:
The paper that put the phrase demographic transition into general circulation, and that framed it as a world process rather than a European peculiarity. Davis opens with the image of population growth as a long, thin powder fuse burning slowly for a million years before reaching the charge and exploding.

Industrialisation gave the impetus in Europe, but its diffusion meant that for the first time the whole of the world's population could be treated as a single entity responding in varying degrees to one dynamic. The transition is therefore staged and diffusionist: the same sequence arrives at different times in different places.
entries.title: The World Demographic Transition
entries.venue: Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science

entries.keyArgument:
High fertility in agrarian societies is not an absence of control but the product of an institutional complex well adapted to a peasant economy: the joint household with three or more generations, early and near-universal marriage, kin authority over reproductive decisions, and the sanctions that make barrenness a household failure.

Because these arrangements distribute the costs of children away from the couple who bear them, fertility stays high without anyone choosing it. The corollary for policy is that fertility falls when the institutional supports are withdrawn, not when motives are addressed one household at a time.
entries.title: Institutional Patterns Favoring High Fertility in Underdeveloped Areas

entries.keyArgument:
The founding text of the economic approach to fertility. Becker treats children as durable goods yielding a stream of satisfactions, so that the number a couple has responds to income, to the price of children relative to other goods, and to knowledge of contraception.

The move that has shaped everything since is the separation of quantity from quality: parents choose not only how many children to have but how much to spend on each, and a rise in income can be taken out largely in quality. This is how Becker reconciles a theoretically positive income effect with the observed negative cross-sectional relationship between income and family size, which he attributes substantially to differences in contraceptive knowledge.
entries.title: An Economic Analysis of Fertility
entries.venue: Demographic and Economic Change in Developed Countries

entries.keyArgument:
Davis's multiphasic response: faced with sustained natural increase and improving survival, families do not select one remedy but reach for every means available at once, postponing marriage, staying single, migrating, aborting, sterilising and contracepting, in whatever combination their circumstances allow.

The motor is not absolute poverty but the threat to relative position: people respond in order to keep or improve their standing as the number of surviving children rises. Demographic change is thus reflexive and behavioural, each component altered by the changes it induces in the others, which is why a single-cause account of the transition will always underfit the record.
entries.title: The Theory of Change and Response in Modern Demographic History

entries.citationNote: Not in your corpus. Added from the published literature; volume and pages should be confirmed against the conference proceedings.
entries.keyArgument:
Written out of the European Fertility Project, which had found that fertility fell across provinces with very different levels of income, urbanisation and mortality, and that it clustered instead by language and culture.

Coale's response is the three preconditions: fertility falls when deliberate control is within the calculus of conscious choice, when reduced fertility is perceived as advantageous, and when effective means are available. The first condition is the one that shifted the field, since it makes the transition partly a question of what is thinkable, which is the door Cleland and Wilson later walk through.
entries.title: The Demographic Transition Reconsidered
entries.venue: Proceedings of the International Population Conference, Liège 1973, vol. 1

entries.keyArgument:
Davis takes the zero-growth debate apart by insisting that a goal is empty until its means are specified. When ZPG was first proposed the goal itself went undefended and only the means were argued about; once it became a movement the argument moved to the goal and the means were left vague.

His position is that voluntary family planning cannot deliver replacement fertility, because the institutional machinery of family life keeps the demand for children at or above it. A serious population policy must therefore work on the structure of incentives surrounding family formation rather than on the supply of contraception, a conclusion that made the paper a standing provocation in the field.
entries.title: Zero Population Growth: The Goal and the Means

entries.citationNote: Not in your corpus. Added from the published literature; volume and pages should be confirmed.
entries.keyArgument:
Bongaarts turns the Davis and Blake intermediate variables into a working accounting framework, reducing them to four indices that between them explain most of the variation in fertility across populations: marriage, contraception, induced abortion and postpartum infecundability.

Its importance is methodological rather than theoretical. Any social or economic determinant must act through these channels, so the framework is the standard bridge between a behavioural explanation and an observed fertility level, and it is what lets a claim about ideas or institutions be checked arithmetically.
entries.title: A Framework for Analyzing the Proximate Determinants of Fertility

entries.keyArgument:
McNicoll opens with the observation that everyone knows why fertility falls with economic development, that Thompson, Lorimer, Notestein and Davis set the reasons out clearly, and that little has been added since. The anomaly he presses is that we nonetheless lack a theory of fertility in any serious sense: a coherent body of analysis linking a characterisation of society and economy to individual fertility decisions and outcomes, able to survive the empirical record.

His answer is to locate the missing link in institutions, the rules and organisational forms that mediate between macro conditions and household decisions, which is why policy inferences drawn from statistical associations between fertility and other variables are so often unreliable. The paper is the founding statement of the institutional approach that Davis had gestured at and that Caldwell and Greenhalgh would develop.
entries.title: Institutional Determinants of Fertility Change

entries.keyArgument:
Davis argues that the breadwinner system, in which the husband earned and the wife did not, was a historically brief arrangement rather than the traditional family, and that its dissolution is the central social fact of the period.

Extrapolating age-specific participation rates for married women from 20 to 44, he projected that married women would match married men's labour force participation by 1998. The consequence he draws is institutional: as the earning role ceases to differentiate spouses, the arrangement that sustained high marital fertility loses its rationale, which places the gender division of labour at the centre of any account of low fertility.
entries.title: Wives and Work: The Sex Role Revolution and Its Consequences

entries.issue: Supplement: Below-Replacement Fertility in Industrial Societies
entries.keyArgument:
Davis sets below-replacement fertility against the whole span of human evolution and finds it anomalous: never in recorded history, not in the Great Depression, not in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, not in ancient times, and not across the millions of years of hominid evolution has fertility been so low for entire societies.

The argument this licenses is that low fertility cannot be explained by any mechanism with deep evolutionary roots, since none produced it before. Something in the modern institutional environment is overriding an evolved reproductive motivation, which makes the phenomenon a puzzle about contemporary institutions rather than about human nature.
entries.title: Low Fertility in Evolutionary Perspective

entries.keyArgument:
The central challenge to the economic account of the transition. Cleland and Wilson assemble the historical European and contemporary developing-country evidence and find that the timing of fertility decline tracks language, region and cultural boundaries more closely than it tracks the economic conditions that demand theories make decisive.

Their alternative is ideational: what spreads is the idea that deliberate control of family size is legitimate and possible, and it spreads along channels of communication and cultural affinity. The paper set the terms for three decades of argument between demand and diffusion explanations, and it remains the standard citation for the view that the transition is a change in what is thinkable rather than in what is affordable.
entries.title: Demand Theories of the Fertility Transition: An Iconoclastic View

entries.citationNote: Not in your corpus. Added from the published literature; issue details should be confirmed.
entries.keyArgument:
The statement that named the second demographic transition and carried it to an international audience. Van de Kaa argues that the changes in European family life after the mid-1960s are not a disturbance in the first transition but a distinct regime: sustained below-replacement fertility, postponed and fewer marriages, cohabitation, childbearing outside marriage, divorce, and effective contraception used for self-realisation rather than family limitation.

The underlying shift he proposes is from an era of concern for the child to one of concern for the self-fulfilment of the adult couple. Burke 2026 and the current low-fertility literature are still arguing with this thesis.
entries.title: Europe's Second Demographic Transition

entries.keyArgument:
Blake gives the quantity–quality tradeoff an empirical edge by showing that the number of siblings is strongly and negatively related to years of schooling and to verbal ability scores, with the penalty concentrated in early truncation of schooling before high school graduation.

She is careful about a point that is often mishandled: the family size of mothers and the sibling number experienced by children diverge, so the decline in completed fertility does not exhaust the change in the environments children grow up in. As sibling numbers fall with very low fertility, the dilution mechanism implies rising attainment and verbal ability for recent cohorts.
entries.title: Number of Siblings and Educational Attainment

entries.citationNote: Not in your corpus. Added from the published literature; volume and pages should be confirmed.
entries.keyArgument:
Greenhalgh argues that fertility decisions are made inside structures of power, and that a demography which treats the household as an undifferentiated decision unit misses the politics inside it as well as the political economy around it.

Her programme is to situate reproductive behaviour in institutional, political and historical context, attending to inequality between generations and between women and men, and to the state's reach into the family. It is the anthropological counterpart to McNicoll's institutional argument, and it supplies the language in which later work on gender and reproduction is written.
entries.title: Toward a Political Economy of Fertility: Anthropological Contributions

entries.keyArgument:
Written for an African audience at the point when Latin America's transition was far enough advanced to be read as a completed case. At the start of the 1960s the region was marked by high population growth, the product of persistently high fertility and an earlier mortality decline, and it was the Latin American experience that gave the demographic explosion much of its urgency.

Coinciding with those same dates, fertility began to fall across most of the region. The paper reconstructs when and under what conditions the decline began, country by country, and asks what in the Latin American onset is transferable to sub-Saharan Africa and what belongs to the region's particular configuration.
entries.title: The Onset of Fertility Decline in Latin America
entries.venue: IUSSP Committee on Comparative Analysis of Fertility; Seminar on the Course of Fertility Transition in Sub-Saharan Africa, Harare, 19–22 November 1991

entries.keyArgument:
The companion piece to Van de Kaa in the same issue, setting out what Latin American research contributed to the analysis of fertility determinants, a body of work largely absent from the anglophone narratives.

Four lines are reconstructed. Fertility as the reproduction of labour power, in Aldunate, Singer, Campanario, de Oliveira and Torrado, where daily and intergenerational reproduction are read through the production process and family types are attached to social classes, down to the ideologically determined familia fetiche. The family as the fundamental unit of analysis, pressing into its internal dynamics rather than treating the couple as a decision unit. The effect of economic transformation, including Bravo's study of Chile from 1960 to 1991 showing how structural adjustment worked through unemployment, wage erosion and income uncertainty. And the urban transition, following Martine on whether urbanisation and fertility transition in Brazil are independent or interdependent processes.
entries.title: El aporte latinoamericano al análisis de los factores determinantes de la fecundidad

entries.keyArgument:
Van de Kaa borrows the anchored-narrative idea from the psychology of courtroom judgement: judges rarely reconstruct what happened by logical inference, they adopt a story and then anchor it in the evidence and in common knowledge of how things usually go. A well-anchored narrative is built from sub-narratives, nested and hierarchical, each requiring anchoring as specific as its claims.

Half a century of research into the determinants of fertility is best read the same way: as a set of sub-narratives developed from different orientations and perspectives, each anchored in a particular region, period and body of evidence. His honest conclusion is that no single good story has been accepted by all specialists about the conditions necessary and sufficient to produce fertility change, and that it no longer seems sensible to seek one theory valid for all regions and all periods.

The Spanish translation of "Anchored Narratives: The Story and Findings of Half a Century of Research into the Determinants of Fertility," Population Studies 50(3), 1996, 389–432.
entries.title: Narraciones ancladas: historia y resultados de medio siglo de investigaciones sobre los determinantes de la fecundidad

entries.citationNote: Not in your corpus. Added from the published literature; volume and pages should be confirmed.
entries.keyArgument:
McDonald's gender-equity thesis, and the most portable explanation of why very low fertility appears where it does. His claim is that fertility falls to very low levels when gender equity in individual-oriented institutions, above all education and the labour market, runs far ahead of gender equity within the family and family-oriented institutions.

Women who are treated as individuals at school and at work and as traditional wives at home respond by having fewer children. The prediction is comparative: southern Europe and East Asia should sit lowest, the Nordic countries higher, which is broadly what the record showed. Andersson's Swedish decline is the case that now strains it.
entries.title: Gender Equity in Theories of Fertility Transition

entries.keyArgument:
Caldwell's collected statement of the wealth-flows programme, gathering the papers on pretransitional control, the supposed Neolithic mortality crisis, intensification, and the restatement of transition theory into a single architecture. The analytical approach set out in chapter 1 is that the type of economy determines the family's reproductive regime, so that hunter-gatherers, farmers and wage earners should be expected to have different demographic regimes rather than points on one scale.

The book is also the place where the programme confronts its critics, which makes it useful less as a summary of transition theory than as a record of what one of its principal architects thought had survived contact with the evidence.
entries.title: Demographic Transition Theory

entries.keyArgument:
Thirty years after the 1976 restatement, Caldwell revisits the claim that before fertility decline uncontrolled fertility is an economically rational choice, given the net value of children's work and their insurance value against danger, disaster and old age.

He argues that the apparently conflicting evidence on the value of children's work is more apparent than real and shows how the findings can be reconciled, and he proposes that a better understanding of the insurance function explains both the reversal of the wealth flow and the speed with which fertility falls once it begins. The chapter is the cleanest place to see what the wealth-flows hypothesis actually commits its author to.
entries.title: On Net Intergenerational Wealth Flows: An Update

entries.keyArgument:
A chronicle of more than fifty states and territories and 564 million people, written against the region's apparent uniformity. The authors insist on its diversity: a long settlement history, the collapse of indigenous populations at contact followed by four further crisis cycles through conquest, the Bourbon reforms, the liberal republics and finally neoliberal adjustment and globalisation, and the massive colonial-era inflows from Europe and Africa.

The demographic account runs from the post-1950 mortality decline through the onset and spread of fertility decline to the migration turn, and it is the standard reference for the regional transition in a comparative frame. Its running argument is that regional aggregates conceal more than they reveal, since the same transition arrives at very different dates and speeds across and within these countries.
entries.title: The Demography of Latin America and the Caribbean since 1950

entries.keyArgument:
The hypothesis that below a certain level low fertility becomes self-reinforcing through three mechanisms that feed one another.

Demographically, fewer women of reproductive age produce fewer births, which shrinks the next cohort again. Sociologically, young people who grow up among small families form lower ideal family sizes, since the ideal is calibrated on what they see. Economically, declining expectations of future income and rising aspirations widen the gap between what young adults want and what they think they can afford.

The second mechanism is the one that matters most for theory, because it makes preferences endogenous to the fertility level itself. Golovina's Finnish cohort findings are close to a direct test.

Not in your corpus; added from the published literature.
entries.title: The Low Fertility Trap Hypothesis: Forces that May Lead to Further Postponement and Fewer Births in Europe

entries.keyArgument:
Divergent fertility outcomes are routinely ascribed to state action, to policy deliberate or inadvertent. McNicoll argues that divergence is often more persuasively traced to initial conditions: cultural and institutional inheritance, the supply of human capital, even features of the natural and built environment. These are the hands societies are dealt, and he groups them under legacy.

Policy and legacy are interwoven, since policy builds on some legacy elements and tries, often ineffectively, to work around others, and neither fully determines outcomes because external pressures and opportunities, which he calls circumstance, also count. Legacy and circumstance can shrink the policy space in ways not apparent to outside observers, which argues for circumspection about past policy failures and for reining in the hopes attached to reform agendas. The contrast he works through is East Asia against sub-Saharan Africa over fifty years.
entries.title: Legacy, Policy, and Circumstance in Fertility Transition

entries.citationNote: Not in your corpus. Added from the published literature; volume and pages should be confirmed.
entries.keyArgument:
Lesthaeghe's own account of where the second demographic transition stood forty years in, and his answer to the charge that it was a description of north-west Europe dressed up as a theory.

He traces the spread of the pattern beyond its origin, including to the United States, central and eastern Europe and East Asia, and defends the ideational core: the rise of higher-order needs, self-realisation and expressive values, anchored in the shift Maslow and Inglehart describe, as the driver behind postponement, cohabitation, non-marital childbearing and sustained low fertility.

The companion piece to Van de Kaa in this index, and the standing statement of the position that Burke 2026 tests against the American plateau.
entries.title: The Unfolding Story of the Second Demographic Transition

entries.citationNote: Not in your corpus. Added from the published literature; volume and pages should be confirmed.
entries.keyArgument:
The standard review of how economic downturns move fertility, assembled from the Great Depression through the recessions of the late twentieth century to the Great Recession.

The regularities they establish are that recessions depress fertility modestly and with a lag, that the effect is concentrated in first births and among the young, that it operates through unemployment and economic uncertainty rather than income alone, and that much of the loss is postponement rather than forgone childbearing.

It is the baseline against which the post-2010 decline looks anomalous, since recovery did not bring the rebound this literature would predict. Vignoli and Andersson both take up the problem it leaves.
entries.title: Economic Recession and Fertility in the Developed World

entries.keyArgument:
The two-halves account of the gender revolution, and the most optimistic of the low-fertility frameworks. The first half moved women into public life, into education and paid work, and it destabilised the family and depressed fertility because nothing compensated at home.

The second half moves men into the private sphere, into housework and care, and the authors argue it should restabilise family life and raise fertility rather than lower it further. Low fertility on this reading is a feature of an incomplete revolution rather than its endpoint.

It is the direct counterweight to McDonald's gender-equity thesis, which stops where this one continues, and the Nordic decline since 2010 is the hardest case for it.

Not in your corpus; added from the published literature.
entries.title: The Gender Revolution: A Framework for Understanding Changing Family and Demographic Behavior

entries.citationNote: Author's pre-final draft, obtained directly from Rotkirch, so the text is reliable. Cite the published chapter in Hopcroft's Oxford Handbook of Evolution, Biology, and Society for pagination, or cite as the author's manuscript version.
entries.keyArgument:
Rotkirch's programmatic statement of evolutionary family sociology, which studies how genetic relatedness and psychological predispositions shape intimate relations, setting human families against other species and the history of hominid evolution.

Two research fields carry the argument. Couple relations, gender equality and involved fatherhood are better understood when sexual selection theory is combined with family system theories. Grandparenting is the second, where Darwinian theory and mainstream family sociology are being integrated around helping, conflict and kin lineages across generations.

The Darwinian side contributes attention to how genetic relatedness shapes familial sentiment and behaviour and to the universal patterns in family dynamics; the sociological side specifies the conditions under which those patterns vary. This is the theoretical apparatus behind her later work on reproductive cues.

The file is the pre-final draft; page numbers should be taken from the published chapter.
entries.title: Evolutionary Family Sociology
entries.venue: The Oxford Handbook of Evolution, Biology, and Society, chapter 21 (ed. Rosemary Hopcroft)

entries.citationNote: Not in your corpus. Added from the published literature; the DOI is confirmed, the page range should be checked.
entries.keyArgument:
Beaujouan and Berghammer compare the family size young people said they wanted with what their cohorts actually achieved, across European countries and the United States, cohort by cohort rather than at a single moment.

The gap between intended and completed fertility has widened over successive cohorts, and the widening comes mostly from the collapse of large families and the growth of childlessness rather than from a shift in what people say they want, which has stayed close to two.

This is the foundational cohort measurement of the aspiration gap, and the empirical companion to Yeatman and Smith-Greenaway's review in this index.
entries.title: The Gap Between Lifetime Fertility Intentions and Completed Fertility in Europe and the United States: A Cohort Approach

entries.keyArgument:
The puzzle is that the pro-cyclical relationship between economic conditions and fertility documented since 1970 broke down after the Great Recession. Northern European economies resumed growth in 2009 while their fertility fell sharply, Norway from 1.98 in 2009 toward 1.6.

Vignoli and colleagues rebuild the decision framework around Knight's distinction between risk, where the probability distribution of future events is known, and uncertainty, where outcomes cannot be estimated by probability calculus or are simply unknown. Under genuine uncertainty people cannot optimise, so they act on narratives of the future: imagined, socially shared accounts of what is coming that render the future available for guidance in the present, in Dewey's phrase.

The chapter sets out the framework, addresses its causal validity, and argues that fertility research must treat expectations about the future as a cause in their own right rather than as noise around objective conditions.
entries.title: Uncertainty and Narratives of the Future: A Theoretical Framework for Contemporary Fertility
entries.venue: Analyzing Contemporary Fertility, chapter 3 (ed. Robert Schoen); Springer Series on Demographic Methods and Population Analysis 51

entries.citationNote: Accepted manuscript obtained directly from the authors, so the text is reliable. Volume and page numbers come from the published Marriage & Family Review version; the DOI resolves to it.
entries.keyArgument:
Finland's total fertility rate fell from 1.87 in 2010 to 1.35 in 2019, one of the steepest declines in Europe. Using Finnish Family Barometer survey data on people aged 20 to 44 who did not plan to have children soon, the authors ask what reasons those people give.

Exploratory factor analysis groups the reasons into three: an uncertain life situation, lifestyle preferences, and completed fertility. A more stable life situation, infrequent social media use and lower work orientation are associated with lower uncertainty, while being a woman, being childless, frequent social media use and higher work orientation are associated with stronger lifestyle preferences.

Uncertainty and lifestyle preferences operate independently of sociodemographic characteristics, which is the finding that resists a purely structural reading of the Nordic decline. Note the social media association, measured rather than asserted.

Volume and page numbers should be taken from the published version.
entries.sourceFile: Savelieva_Accepted_manuscript.pdf (accepted manuscript, obtained from the authors)
entries.title: Reasons to postpone childbearing during fertility decline in Finland

entries.keyArgument:
US birth rates fell sharply after 2007 and did not recover as the economy did. Kearney, Levine and Pardue test the obvious candidates against the data and rule them out one by one: the decline is not explained by the business cycle, by housing or student debt, by contraceptive access, by the cost of childcare, by Medicaid or by shifts in the composition of the population.

The decline is broad, appearing across almost every group, and concentrated in first births to young women. What is left, on their account, are shifting priorities across cohorts, which is an explanation by elimination rather than by evidence.

The American statement of the same puzzle Andersson poses for Sweden, and the reason the attitudinal literature grew after it.

Not in your corpus; added from the published literature.
entries.title: The Puzzle of Falling US Birth Rates since the Great Recession

entries.keyArgument:
Fertility fell in every developed country, but not on the same schedule: some nations crossed into "lowest-low" fertility (below 1.3) by the 1990s while others with similar starting points in the 1980s did not. Goldin argues the decisive variable is the speed of postwar economic growth — countries that experienced rapid GNP-per-capita growth after a long period of stagnation saw material conditions change faster than beliefs, values and traditions could adjust.

That mismatch between fast-moving economics and slow-moving norms generates generational and gender conflict specifically in the rapid-growth cases, which is her explanation for why the crossover into lowest-low fertility clustered around the 1980s and 1990s for one group of countries and never happened for the other. A direct, dated answer to the puzzle of timing that most fertility-decline theories leave unaddressed.
entries.title: Babies and the Macroeconomy
entries.venue: NBER Working Paper 33311 (rev. May 2025); forthcoming, Economica

entries.keyArgument:
Using the Finnish Family Barometers across five birth cohorts from 1970–1974 to 1990–1994, the authors find that the ideal number of children is lower in more recent cohorts, and that the shift is driven substantially by a rise in child-free ideals rather than by a general move toward smaller families.

Socioeconomic factors are associated with ideals, but the cohort differences remain significant once they are controlled, which is the finding that matters for theory: what has changed is not only the capacity to realise a family but the family people say they want. This is the empirical anchor for treating the post-2010 decline as a change in preferences rather than in constraints.
entries.title: Birth cohort changes in fertility ideals: evidence from repeated cross-sectional surveys in Finland

entries.keyArgument:
The social sciences have produced an impressive body of research on the determinants of fertility, yet those determinants and the theories behind them are rarely evaluated on their ability to predict new data. Without that test, studies cannot be systematically compared and knowledge does not accumulate.

The authors present two datasets for the PreFer data challenge: one from the LISS panel, with thousands of variables including preferences and values, and one from Dutch register data. The challenge asks whether fertility outcomes can be predicted at all, and which family of predictors does better.

For a literature built on explanation rather than prediction, this is a methodological provocation as much as a resource: it makes the predictive weakness of established determinants visible and measurable.
entries.title: Combining the strengths of Dutch survey and register data in a data challenge to predict fertility (PreFer)

entries.keyArgument:
Israel is the OECD's fertility outlier — pronatalist norms hold across educational and religiosity lines, and fertility has risen alongside rising education and delayed childbearing, the reverse of the pattern seen almost everywhere else in the developed world. This annual overview tracks how the war years disrupted and then restored that pattern: Jewish fertility dipped at the war's outset before rebounding to roughly 3.10 children per woman, while immigration remained robust, with notable inflows from North America and Western Europe.

The report also complicates the exceptionalism story internally: peripheral and non-Haredi Jewish communities are growing more slowly than settlement areas in Judea and Samaria, and the northern regions show a pre-war stagnation the author flags as needing attention in postwar reconstruction. Read alongside the Confucian-paradox and family-institutions literature already in this corpus, Israel is the sharpest available test case for any theory claiming an ideational field must weaken as societies modernize.
entries.publisher: Taub Center for Social Policy Studies in Israel
entries.title: Demography Overview, 2024: Diverging Fertility, Shifting Migration, and Shrinking Yishuvim

entries.keyArgument:
The closing chapter argues that state-reproduction relationships have mostly been discussed through overarching paradigmatic ideas about how a national body should reproduce, so that the regulation of reproduction is treated as a by-product of ideological projects such as nationalism or pronatalism.

Without denying the central role of normative ideas, Zagel and Almeling argue that this focus has obscured the instruments themselves: how ideas translate into goals, what instruments are used, and how coherent instruments and goals actually are.

The stakes are immediate. Governments facing declining birth rates are searching for ways to raise fertility at the same moment as advocates are naming injustices in how states bestow reproductive rights differentially across social groups, from the financing of contraception and abortion care to selective access. Treating these as one policy field rather than two is the contribution.
entries.title: Discussion: reproduction policy in the twenty-first century
entries.venue: Reproduction Policy in the Twenty-First Century: A Comparative Analysis (ed. Hannah Zagel)

entries.keyArgument:
Canada's total fertility rate fell from 1.69 in 2008 to 1.33 by 2022, and Teng and Margolis decompose that fall into its quantum and tempo components. Sixty-one percent of the decline reflects falling quantum — women simply having fewer children over their lifetimes — while only 39 percent reflects tempo effects, the postponement of births to later ages.

The single largest contributor is the decline in first births among women aged 18 to 28, which concentrates the story on young women choosing not to start families at ages that were once the norm, rather than on higher-order births disappearing among women who already have one child. This gives Canada a similar quantum-dominant profile to Uruguay's big decline also in this corpus, distinct from countries where postponement alone can explain most of the fall.
entries.title: Fertility Decline in Canada Since the Great Recession

entries.keyArgument:
A comprehensive review of the economics literature on low fertility in high-income countries: what drives it, what it costs, and what can be done. The authors work through the standard drivers — rising opportunity costs of childbearing, housing and childcare costs, delayed partnership, uncertainty — without treating any single one as sufficient on its own.

Their distinctive contribution is on consequences and policy: they trace through aging, shrinking labor supply, and fiscal strain on pension and health systems, then argue that thoughtful, consistent policy design can mitigate most of these adverse economic consequences even without reversing the fertility decline itself. Useful as a state-of-the-field reference for the economic-consequences side of the literature, distinct from the many entries in this corpus focused on causes of the decline rather than its downstream effects.
entries.title: Fertility in High-Income Countries: Trends, Patterns, Determinants, and Consequences

entries.keyArgument:
An edited comparative volume treating reproduction policy as a policy field in its own right rather than as an appendix to family or social policy. Open access from Edward Elgar.

The organising move is to bring together the instruments that states use across the whole span of reproduction, from contraception and abortion through assisted reproduction to the support of childbearing, and to compare them as a set. That framing cuts across the usual separation between pronatalist policy on one side and reproductive rights on the other.
entries.publisher: Edward Elgar Publishing, Cheltenham and Northampton MA
entries.title: Reproduction Policy in the Twenty-First Century: A Comparative Analysis

entries.keyArgument:
Uruguay's total fertility rate fell from 2.0 to 1.37 children per woman in just six years, 2015 to 2021 — among the fastest six-year drops recorded anywhere. The authors trace it to postponement of births, concentrated among adolescents and young women, compounding with a separate decline in higher-order births among older mothers; mean age at first birth rose by almost two years over the period.

Their cautious closing note is that the decline may already be stabilizing, with some potential for a modest rebound as postponed births are eventually realized — a hypothesis this corpus's period/cohort distinction (see Onofri et al. and Geruso-Spears) helps make precise: a period-rate collapse this steep can overstate the fall in completed cohort fertility if postponement is later recuperated.
entries.title: The Big Decline: Lowest-Low Fertility in Uruguay (2016–2021)

entries.keyArgument:
The first systematic cross-country accounting of the Arab world's fertility decline, using World Bank data across 2011 to 2021. The pattern is uneven rather than uniform: Jordan (down 24.3 percent), Iraq (22.2 percent) and Yemen (19.1 percent) saw the steepest falls, while Libya, Tunisia, Lebanon and Kuwait declined only slightly (around 4 to 5 percent), and Algeria showed essentially no decline over the decade. The UAE already held the region's lowest rate throughout the period, while Somalia remained the highest.

The paper does not offer a causal mechanism so much as establish the descriptive baseline this corpus otherwise lacks for the region: which Arab states are converging toward low fertility, which are not, and how large the gap between them already is.
entries.title: The Epidemiological Declining in the Human Fertility Rate in the Arab World for 10 Years Period 2011–2021

entries.keyArgument:
A qualitative exploratory study commissioned by the Chilean finance ministry, set against a fall in the total fertility rate from 5.4 in 1960 to 1.16 in 2023 and a preliminary 1.03 in 2024, which places Chile among the lowest-fertility countries in the world.

The framing is what distinguishes it: alongside the fiscal and labour-force consequences, the report names a crisis of reproductive freedom, the inability of the population to realise its own reproductive aspirations under structural, cultural and economic constraints. It notes that unlike other OECD countries Chile faces this decline without a clear diagnosis and without a dedicated policy framework, and it closes with recommendations drawn from that gap.
entries.publisher: Ministerio de Hacienda de Chile, Coordinación de Género y Laboratorio de Gobierno
entries.title: Análisis de las condicionantes y los desafíos de la natalidad en Chile

entries.keyArgument:
Geruso and Spears decompose the fall in cohort fertility below replacement into two distinct components that are often conflated: growing childlessness, and fewer children among women who have at least one. Using data spanning Europe, North and South America, Southeast Asia, and Indian districts, they find childlessness explains only 38 percent of the decline in advanced economies, and just 6 percent in the Indian context they study.

The bulk of the below-replacement decline, in other words, comes from parity progression — women having a first child but stopping sooner — not from a rising share never having children at all. This cuts against narratives that treat rising childlessness as the primary engine of the decline, and redirects attention toward whatever discourages a second or third birth once a first has occurred.
entries.title: Childless or Child-fewer? Childlessness and Parity Progression where Fertility Is Below Replacement

entries.keyArgument:
Using qualitative policy case studies across China, Japan and South Korea, the authors examine falling fertility not as a single national trend but as a pattern of "stratified reproduction" — the unequal valuing and support of different women's reproduction, a concept they trace to Colen (1995) and Ginsburg and Rapp (1995).

Across all three countries, fertility has fallen most sharply among women with lower education, income and job security: in Korea, women with only elementary education recorded a fertility rate of 0.17 in 2021 against a national rate of 0.78, while higher-educated Japanese women saw modest fertility gains even as the overall pattern kept falling. The authors argue pronatalist policy in all three states largely overlooks these intersectional structural barriers, and that reproduction being an individual right does not by itself guarantee universal support for exercising it — a comprehensive, not merely rhetorical, policy response is needed.
entries.title: Declining Fertility Rates and Stratified Reproduction among Women in East Asia: What Can We Learn from the Cases of China, Japan and South Korea?

authors: Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean
entries.keyArgument:
The region's own statistical and policy body documents what is now a decade-old below-replacement trend: total fertility has been under 2.1 across Latin America and the Caribbean since 2015, reaching 1.8 in Latin America and just 1.5 in the Caribbean by 2024.

The report goes beyond the aggregate number to examine socioeconomic inequality in reproductive behavior within countries and to survey family-policy responses across the region. As the direct institutional successor to the CELADE reports already in this corpus (Guzmán and colleagues, 1991–2006), it extends that same regional tradition of tracking the transition into the low-fertility era the earlier reports could only anticipate.
entries.publisher: Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC/CEPAL)
entries.title: Demographic Observatory 2025: Low Fertility in Latin America and the Caribbean — Emerging Trends and Dynamics

entries.keyArgument:
Fitting a Markov switching model to South Korean fertility data from 1960 to 2023, Ayodeji identifies two structurally distinct regimes rather than one continuous decline: a sharp 17.3 percent annual fall from 1960 to 1988, driven by the classic transition mechanisms, followed by a much more gradual 2.5 percent annual decline from 1989 onward that behaves like a different process entirely.

The second regime shows smaller fluctuations and a 56.3 percent estimated probability of persisting, which the author reads as statistical support for the low-fertility trap hypothesis — the idea that once a society settles into sufficiently low fertility, self-reinforcing mechanisms (smaller reference-group family sizes, eroded family-formation institutions) make a return to higher fertility structurally difficult regardless of policy. The distinction between the two regimes is a useful corrective to treating South Korea's decline as one continuous process amenable to one continuous explanation.
entries.title: Empirical Insights into South Korea's Persistent Low Fertility and the Path Forward for Pro-Natalist Policies

entries.keyArgument:
Against accounts that treat the fertility crisis as purely social and economic, this paper marshals evidence that biological fecundity itself is declining. Markers of decreased fecundity — poor semen quality, rising female infertility — are increasing, alongside a growing share of couples needing medically assisted reproduction.

The paper's methodological contribution is a new index, the comprehensive unassisted pregnancy rate (live births plus induced abortions, excluding births via assisted reproduction), meant to isolate a population's underlying fecundity from its fertility behavior. In the handful of high-income countries where it can be constructed, this rate has been declining steadily across successive decades — a trend that cannot be explained by postponement or preference alone, and that most of the social-science literature on fertility decline does not engage with at all.
entries.title: Evidence That Declining Human Fecundity Contributes to the Fertility Crisis

entries.keyArgument:
Macro-level gender-equity theory, most associated with McDonald, predicts that fertility should stabilize or rise once societies combine gender equality in public institutions with gender equality inside the family. Denmark, Finland and Norway are among the most gender-equal societies in the world by any standard measure, and their fertility has been falling all the same — the paradox the title names.

Using a multidimensional gender-equality-attitudes instrument from the 2020–2022 Generations and Gender Programme across all three countries (n=13,184), Begall and Hiekel find distinct attitude profiles among respondents that relate clearly to fertility intentions among the childless, even though the countries' aggregate gender-equality scores would predict otherwise. The implication is that macro-level gender-equity theory may be too coarse an instrument: what matters is not a country's gender-equality score but which specific configuration of gender attitudes an individual holds.
entries.title: Examining the Gender Equality–Fertility Paradox in Three Nordic Countries

entries.keyArgument:
Where research on the 2000s highlighted reductions in higher-order births and first-birth postponement as the joint drivers of Latin America's fertility decline, this paper isolates what changed in the following decade. Using period-, age-, and order-specific rates across six countries representing roughly three-quarters of the region's population, plus Latinx populations in the United States, the authors find that 49 to 85 percent of the 2011–2020 decline is concentrated in the youngest age groups.

The implication is a shift in mechanism: first-birth postponement, not reduced higher-order childbearing, is now the primary engine of the region's continuing fall into low and lowest-low fertility. Read against the Onofri-Berniell-Fernández-Menduiña NBER paper also in this corpus, the two studies converge on postponement and within-group change as the region's dominant story, rather than compositional shifts in education or urbanization.
entries.title: Fertility Decline to Low and Lowest-Low Levels in Latin America

entries.keyArgument:
A regional report covering all five Central Asian states finds a demographic bloc that can no longer be described with one number. Uzbekistan's total fertility rate continues to rise, reaching 3.4 in 2023, the highest in the region, even as Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan approach or dip under replacement level and births in Kazakhstan itself are already declining.

The divergence matters for any theory of fertility transition timing: five countries with a shared Soviet institutional inheritance and broadly similar starting conditions three decades ago are now on visibly different trajectories, which argues against reading "post-Soviet space" as a single explanatory category the way "East Asia" or "Western Europe" sometimes are in this literature.
entries.publisher: UNICEF Regional Office for Europe and Central Asia
entries.title: Generation 2050 in Central Asia: Interim Regional Report

entries.keyArgument:
Using Brazil's consorcio housing-credit lotteries as a natural experiment — participants pool contributions and periodically receive housing credit by random draw — the authors isolate a causal effect of housing access on fertility that observational studies cannot cleanly identify. Winning housing credit raises the average probability of having a child by 3.8 percent and completed children by 3.2 percent.

The effect is sharply concentrated by age: for 20-to-25-year-olds the increase in probability and children is 32 to 33 percent, while above age 40 there is no detectable effect at all. It is also strongest among lower-income households and those in poor-quality or high-rent housing, exactly where a housing constraint on family formation should bind hardest. This is among the cleanest causal evidence in the corpus that a specific material constraint — not merely correlated with fertility but experimentally shown to affect it — can suppress childbearing among the young in particular.
entries.title: Housing and Fertility

entries.keyArgument:
Using Generations and Gender Survey data collected during and after the COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2023) across eleven European countries, Friedrich and Bujard compare three distinct measures that are often conflated: intended, ideal, and actual family size, broken out by age group.

Intended family size among 18-to-29-year-olds ranges widely, from 1.82 in Finland to 2.47 in Moldova, and the gap between women's mean ideal and actual family size at ages 40 to 49 ranges from 0.42 to 0.63 children depending on the country. The determinants shift across the life course: religiosity matters most for intentions formed early, while education matters most during the primary family-formation phase. The multi-country, multi-measure design makes this a useful empirical anchor for any claim about where in the life course a fertility gap actually opens.
entries.publisher: Bundesinstitut für Bevölkerungsforschung (Federal Institute for Population Research, Germany)
entries.title: Intended, Ideal, and Actual Fertility in 11 European Countries: Evidence on Fertility Gaps in Different Age Groups from the Generations and Gender Survey

entries.keyArgument:
Cevik inverts the usual causal question in fertility-and-growth work: rather than asking how growth affects fertility, he asks how fertility affects growth. Using a panel of 42 European countries from 1960 to 2022 and an instrumental-variable strategy — a comparative index of abortion-law liberalization as an instrument for the total fertility rate — he finds a significant positive effect of fertility on real GDP per capita growth.

The paper is squarely in the economic-demand tradition but points policy attention toward the growth costs of continued fertility decline, giving the "lost generations" framing a quantitative causal claim rather than a demographic projection alone.
entries.title: Lost Generations? Fertility and Economic Growth in Europe

entries.keyArgument:
Surveying 7,967 Russians in May 2023, during the economic and social shock of the war in Ukraine, the authors find that standard demographic predictors of fertility intentions — age, marital status, parenthood status — carry less explanatory weight than subjective and emotional factors. Women's fertility decisions in particular track positive emotional states, happiness and a sense of peacefulness, more closely than men's do.

Political anxiety, conflict-related stress and emotional state are found to amplify one another rather than operating as separate, additive pressures, and trust in state policy emerges as a factor that smooths the population's reaction to shocks. A rare scholarly window into fertility decision-making under acute, state-driven uncertainty, complementing this corpus's Vignoli-school narratives-of-the-future framework with a case where the uncertainty is not economic but political and existential.
entries.title: Periods of High Uncertainty: How Fertility Intentions in Russia Changed During 2022–2023

entries.keyArgument:
A systematic review of China's decade of pronatalist policy shifts — from the universal two-child policy in 2015 to the three-child policy in 2021 — against the plain fact that none of it reversed the fertility decline or restored population growth. Written explicitly to draw lessons for U.S. policymakers, the report treats China's experience as a natural experiment in the limits of state-directed family-size policy.

Its value for this corpus is less any single mechanism than the scale of the null result: a state with far more policy instruments at its disposal than most democracies, deployed with real urgency over ten years, still could not move fertility. That sets a high bar for the plausibility of any weaker, softer pronatalist intervention elsewhere.
entries.title: Pronatalist Pivot: Assessing China's Policy Efforts to Boost Fertility

entries.keyArgument:
Part of a Lancet Regional Health series on low birth rates in the Asia-Pacific, this review reconstructs six decades of fertility trends across East, Southeast and South Asia and asks what drove them at the level of social structure rather than individual choice.

The comparative frame is the contribution: rather than treating East Asia's ultra-low fertility as a single regional story, Yeung and Abalos trace how education expansion, marriage timing, labor-market structure and family policy produced distinct trajectories across three sub-regions that are often collapsed together in the broader "Asian fertility decline" narrative.
entries.title: Social Determinants of Low Fertility in Asia: A Comparative Review of Trends in East, Southeast and South Asia
entries.venue: The Lancet Regional Health – Western Pacific

entries.keyArgument:
Using the Dutch LISS panel and joint latent class analysis, Ivanova identifies distinct trajectories of fertility expectations among childless women and men of reproductive age, modelling them while accounting for respondents who became parents during observation.

Three classes emerge for both sexes: committed to parenthood, the largest; uncertain, at 24 per cent of women and 22 per cent of men; and early commitment to no expectation, at 13.3 and 9.4 per cent. Men show a fourth, later arrivals to expectation of parenthood.

The finding that matters for the pessimism literature is narrower than the framing usually allows. Significant differences by societal pessimism appear only among women: those committed to parenthood report the lowest pessimism and the uncertain group the highest, and the difference survives adjustment for depression, income satisfaction, partnership status and education. Uncertainty, not refusal, is where societal pessimism shows up.
entries.title: Societal pessimism and trajectories of fertility expectations among Dutch non-parents

entries.keyArgument:
UNFPA's flagship annual report reframes the entire policy conversation: the real crisis, it argues, is not demographic decline but a crisis of reproductive agency — the inability of people to have the families they actually want, in either direction. A 14-country YouGov survey commissioned for the report finds that close to 20 percent of reproductive-age adults expect to have fewer children than they desire, with financial limitations, job insecurity and housing concerns cited as the largest obstacles.

The report's policy conclusion runs directly counter to pronatalist alarm: rather than engineering fertility rates upward, states should expand people's real capacity to decide the number, spacing and timing of their children. As the sector's most widely cited annual statement, this gives the corpus's population-policy camp its most prominent recent global counterweight to demographic-collapse framing.
entries.title: State of World Population 2025: The Real Fertility Crisis — The Pursuit of Reproductive Agency in a Changing World

entries.keyArgument:
A comparative cross-sectional study set against Iran's 2022 restriction of contraceptive access, part of the country's broader pronatalist turn. In the Ardabil study population, the policy shifted women away from effective contraception toward less reliable traditional methods, and the reproductive-health consequences were immediate and measurable: unwanted pregnancies rose from 28.5 to 49.25 percent, and abortions from 14.25 to 21.75 percent.

The paper is a sharply measured case of a pronatalist restriction working against its own stated purpose — rather than converting unwanted non-pregnancy into wanted childbearing, restricting contraception appears mainly to have converted planned non-pregnancy into unplanned pregnancy and abortion. A useful counterweight to any account of pronatalist policy that assumes restricting family planning straightforwardly raises fertility.
entries.title: The Impact of New Population Policies on Women's Reproductive Health Pattern in Ardabil, Iran: A Comparative Cross-Sectional Study

entries.keyArgument:
Covering Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Costa Rica and Uruguay from 2010 to 2022, this paper asks a question the aggregate national TFR numbers cannot answer on their own: is the fall into very low fertility mainly a compositional effect — more women becoming educated, and educated women already having fewer children — or is fertility falling within every educational group regardless of composition?

Applying a Kitagawa decomposition across the five countries, the authors find fertility declining across all educational levels in nearly all countries, with the sharpest declines among less-educated women specifically — the opposite of what a pure composition story would predict, since a shrinking less-educated population having many fewer children contributes more to the aggregate fall than education-driven population shifts alone. Read alongside the Onofri-Berniell-Fernández-Menduiña and Arana-Ovalle entries in this corpus, this strengthens the case that within-group change, not compositional shift, is driving Latin America's fertility collapse.
entries.title: The Recent Decline to Very Low Fertility Levels by Education in Five Latin American Countries (2010–2022)

entries.keyArgument:
A narrative review of demographic research on unrealized fertility, the experience of having fewer children than desired, which has expanded rapidly in low-fertility settings and has more recently been shown to be widespread in higher-fertility contexts too, across diverse sociodemographic conditions.

The authors' complaint is that the literature remains fragmented across definitions and measurement approaches with little synthesis between settings. They work through aggregate and individual-level measurement, the difficulty of measuring the same construct across contexts, and the causes.

Three directions are proposed for future work: the consequences of unrealized fertility rather than only its extent, men's unrealized fertility, and unrealized fertility beyond numbers alone, meaning the timing, partner and circumstances people wanted and did not get. The best current map of the gap between desired and achieved fertility.
entries.title: Unrealized fertility in demography

entries.keyArgument:
Tracing Mexico's fertility transition from 1930 to 2015 across four distinct population groups — urban and rural, Indigenous and non-Indigenous — the authors find a concentric diffusion pattern: fertility decline spread outward geographically and socially from urban, high-status municipalities, consistent with prestige-bias and conformism-bias mechanisms of cultural transmission.

The four groups did not transition in lockstep. Urban non-Indigenous populations moved fastest; rural non-Indigenous groups stagnated for a period; rural Indigenous populations experienced delayed onset; and urban Indigenous groups showed the most sustained resistance to decline. The finding complicates a simple socioeconomic-status account of the transition — status predicts the decline's direction consistently, but not its timing or pace, once ethnicity and geography are allowed to interact with it.
entries.title: Unveiling Mexico's Demographic Transitions

entries.keyArgument:
Kearney and Levine document the now-familiar facts — falling total fertility and rising lifetime childlessness across wealthy nations — and then argue against explaining them with a purely economic model of costs and constraints.

Their account centers on a broad shift in priorities: evolving norms around work, gender roles, and an expanded menu of lifestyle options have together reduced how central parenthood is to a well-lived life, for reasons that resist reduction to price and income effects alone. The paper reads as a deliberate rebuttal to demand-theory accounts that expect income and cost shocks to do most of the explanatory work.
entries.title: Why Is Fertility So Low in High-Income Countries?

entries.keyArgument:
A quarter-century after the term was coined, Gietel-Basten and Pardo argue that "lowest-low fertility" (originally, a total fertility rate at or below 1.3) has stopped doing useful analytical work. The label was built to flag a shared alarm, not a shared future, and it now groups countries with very different migration regimes, mortality trajectories, human-capital endowments and institutional capacities under one number.

Their proposed replacement is explicitly multidimensional: understanding a population's actual trajectory requires migration, mortality reduction, human capital and institutions treated as co-equal with fertility itself, not as footnotes to it. The paper is best read as a corrective to any account of "post-transitional" societies that still reasons primarily from the TFR.
entries.title: Beyond Lowest-Low Fertility: Why Post-Transitional Populations Follow Divergent Paths

entries.keyArgument:
Since 2006, Mexico's drug war has driven homicide rates to levels that reshaped mortality and migration across the country, yet whether the resulting violence affected fertility was largely untested. Using administrative birth, death and homicide data for 2,443 municipalities from 2000 to 2020, fixed-effects models and a staggered difference-in-differences design, the authors find essentially no average effect of homicide rates on the total fertility rate, crude birth rate, or fertility desires.

The one partial exception is that municipalities hit by very large homicide spikes between 2010 and 2015 saw slightly faster fertility decline than otherwise similar places. The headline finding is a null result the authors describe as "remarkable continuity": Mexico's ongoing structural fertility decline proceeded on trend largely undisturbed by an extreme, geographically concentrated mortality shock, which argues against treating community violence as a first-order driver of fertility change even where the violence is severe.
entries.title: Changes in Fertility Trends and Women's Fertility Desires in the Wake of the Homicide Surge in Mexico

entries.keyArgument:
After more than fifty years of increase, the share of United States births to unmarried women stalled at around 40 per cent from 2009, a plateau that had gone largely unexamined. Burke shows that this deviation runs against both the deinstitutionalisation-of-marriage thesis and Second Demographic Transition expectations, which anticipated continued decoupling of marriage from childbearing.

Her reading is that marriage has become more rather than less relevant to childbearing, plausibly because economic resources now gate both: the economic bar to marriage has risen at the same time as a bar to childbearing has emerged, and in the absence of subsidised childcare or paid leave people team up to clear them together.
entries.title: Decoupled? The Persistent Relevance of Marriage for Childbearing in the 2010s United States

entries.keyArgument:
Between 2012 and 2022 the ideal number of children fell from 2.42 to 2.31 and the share intending a child within three years fell from 28 to 21 per cent. Using two cross-national surveys each fielded twice about a decade apart, the authors decompose these declines across a competing set of attitudes, theme by theme and then in a horse race.

Three attitudes dominate. Children are increasingly seen as interfering with parents' freedom; views on whether mothers of young children should work have become markedly more progressive, accounting for a larger share of the decline among the tertiary-educated; and fewer people believe that a woman or a man needs children to lead a fulfilled life. That last attitude changed most over the decade and is the largest single contributor to falling intended fertility, above all among less-educated women. The division of household work and work-family conflict contribute little once gender norms enter the competition.
entries.title: Falling Fertility: The Changing Value of Freedom, Fulfillment, and Family

entries.keyArgument:
Cross-country variation in fertility fits the classic theories well enough, but within countries the fertility declines of the last sixty years are on average not associated with greater improvements in human capital, income or survival. Sub-Saharan Africa declined less than predicted, parts of Asia and Latin America more.

Gobbi, Hannusch and Rossi argue that marriage and inheritance customs account for much of the residual. Polygamy, bride price and rivalry between co-wives raise desired fertility and help explain today's stalled African transitions, while partible versus impartible inheritance helps explain the timing of historical declines across premodern European regions. The paper is the current statement of the family-institutions position in economics, and a useful bridge to the ideational literature.
entries.title: Family Institutions and the Global Fertility Transition

entries.keyArgument:
Applying Bongaarts's proximate-determinants framework to 19 major sub-Saharan African cities spanning different stages of the fertility transition, the authors ask which mechanism does the work at each stage rather than treating the transition as one uniform process. Contraceptive use accounts for most of the early decline as cities first begin falling from high fertility, explaining 20 to 32 percent of variation depending on the transition stage examined.

But once cities reach the advanced, late-transition stage, marriage patterns — delayed marriage age, changing union types — take over as the dominant mechanism sustaining lower fertility, accounting for roughly 38 percent of the fertility gap between post-transition and late-transition cities. This is the corpus's most direct empirical test of which African cities have actually reached an "advanced" transition and what is holding their fertility down once they get there, rather than treating Sub-Saharan Africa as uniformly high-fertility.
entries.title: Fertility Transition Across Major Sub-Saharan African Cities: The Role of Proximate Determinants

entries.keyArgument:
Andersson sets out what is known about Sweden's post-2010 decline and reaches a conclusion that constrains any theory of the current downturn. The change can be attributed entirely to a reduced inclination to become a parent: once a first child is born, progression to a second and third is roughly as before.

The fall in first-birth rates is close to uniform across socioeconomic groups and types of residential area, cannot be linked to any deterioration in economic conditions over the period, and is not due to a decline in couple formation. What has changed is the willingness of cohabiting couples to make long-term commitments. Structural factors are no longer sufficient, and the explanation must be sought in subjective factors operating at a general, global level.
entries.publisher: Ministry of Health and Social Affairs, Stockholm
entries.title: From relatively high to declining fertility rates: What happened in Sweden?
entries.venue: Committee for a Future with Children, Publication 2026:2

entries.keyArgument:
Rising education is one of the most common explanations offered for falling fertility, but studies rarely separate two distinct things bundled inside it: the temporary effect of being enrolled in education right now, which mechanically delays childbearing, and the permanent effect of the education ultimately attained, which may or may not lower completed fertility independent of enrollment timing.

Decomposing Norway's fertility decline along exactly this line, Beck, Hellstrand and Myrskylä isolate how much each component contributes. The distinction matters for policy and theory alike: an enrollment-driven decline is compatible with fertility recovering once study periods end, while an attainment-driven decline implies something more permanent about how higher education itself reshapes family-size preferences or capacities, regardless of when it was completed.
entries.title: More Education and Fewer Children? The Contribution of Educational Enrollment and Attainment to the Fertility Decline in Norway

entries.keyArgument:
Most work on social support and childbearing is individual-level; this paper asks whether the social character of a place is associated with its fertility. Drawing social indicators from a national survey of 100,750 adults and fertility from population registers across 299 Finnish municipalities, and using spatial autoregressive error models to absorb spatial autocorrelation between neighbouring municipalities, the authors find that regions with higher social capital have higher total fertility rates.

The contribution to the low-fertility debate is to make social context an ecological variable: the resource in question is not only the support an individual receives but the density of social interaction and participation in the surrounding community.
entries.title: Regional social capital and fertility rate: Municipality-level analysis in Finland

entries.keyArgument:
Secularization is well established as a force in historical Western fertility patterns and almost absent from explanations of the recent declines. Schubert, Skirbekk and Nisén take it up for Finland from 1995 to 2019, using church tax payments in the administrative registers to identify religious affiliation.

The analysis is dyadic rather than individual: it looks at couples' joint religious affiliation, religiously homogeneous and mixed, and their probability of a first birth. The mechanism proposed is self-reinforcing, since declining church membership changes both the childbearing of couples and the composition of the partner market that forms them.

They conclude that the accelerated decline in church membership contributed to Finland's recent fertility decline, which puts a concrete ideational mechanism under the Nordic puzzle that Andersson leaves open.
entries.title: Secularization and low fertility: How declining church membership changes couples' childbearing

entries.keyArgument:
Drawing on the Rapporto Giovani 2022 survey across Italy, France, Germany and Spain, and a sample of 2,616 childless adults aged 25 to 34, the authors ask whether seeing childbearing as a route to self-fulfilment changes how expected welfare-state childcare support translates into fertility intentions, and whether that depends on postmaterialist values.

They model how the self-fulfilment valuation of parenthood varies by postmaterialism and welfare expectations, then estimate a moderated mediation through generalised structural equation modelling with nonparametric bootstrap.

The interest for policy is the implied conditionality: childcare support does not act on intentions directly so much as through what parenthood is taken to mean, so the same provision can land very differently depending on the values of those receiving it.
entries.title: Self-Fulfillment and Fertility Intentions: The Interplay of Postmaterialism and Expected Welfare State Support

entries.keyArgument:
East Asian fertility has fallen to levels without historical precedent in a region whose Confucian heritage placed extraordinary weight on family continuity. Fang and Liu dissolve the paradox by separating two strands of that tradition and noting that modernisation affected them differently.

The pronatal strand, resting on lineage continuity, ancestor worship and reliance on sons in old age, was switched off as child mortality fell, incomes rose, women entered the labour force and state pensions displaced the family. What survived was the veneration of education and of status won by examination. Under a modern single-ranking tournament that strand reverses sign: where the imperial system rewarded having many sons so that one might succeed, the gaokao and suneung reward concentrating resources on one or two intensively educated children, and the quantity–quality tradeoff turns a pro-natal culture into an engine of low fertility.

Prepared for New Frontiers in Fertility, edited by James J. Heckman.
entries.title: The Confucian Fertility Paradox: Education Competition and Ultra-Low Fertility in East Asia

entries.keyArgument:
Most accounts of a fertility transition track the mean number of children per woman as it falls. Batyra and Wilson ask a structurally different question: what happens to the distribution of reproduction across the population as that mean declines — does parenthood become more evenly spread across women, or does it concentrate among a shrinking share who have children while a growing share have none or very few?

For Brazil, they document a declining spread of parenthood as the transition proceeds, meaning the population is not converging on a smaller shared family size so much as diverging into more differentiated reproductive outcomes. This reframes the standard transition narrative: the interesting variation is not only in how many children the average woman has, but in how unequally reproduction itself comes to be distributed as fertility falls.
entries.title: The Distribution of Reproduction during a Fertility Transition: Declining Spread of Parenthood in Brazil

entries.keyArgument:
Distinguishing cohort from period fertility measures, Geruso and Spears note a pattern that argues against treating today's low fertility as a temporary dip: where cohort birth rates have fallen low, they have not subsequently rebounded. That asymmetry — easy to fall, hard to recover — is the paper's central empirical claim.

The decline they trace runs through both channels at once: rising lifetime childlessness and smaller completed families among those who do have children. Read alongside their companion NBER working paper on the same decomposition, this JEP piece is the accessible synthesis aimed at a general economics readership rather than a specialist one, but its "has not rebounded" framing adds something the working paper does not emphasize as sharply.
entries.title: The Likelihood of Persistently Low Global Fertility

entries.keyArgument:
Goldin locates the decline of fertility in a widening mismatch between men's and women's preferences over the terms of a traditional division of labor. As women's autonomy rose — through education, earnings potential and the ability to support themselves independently — the old arrangement stopped being one women would simply accept, while men, who benefited more from preserving it, were slower to renegotiate its terms.

Faced with a partner market that has not adjusted as fast as their own aspirations, career-oriented women increasingly forgo or postpone parenthood rather than accept a bargain that no longer reflects their bargaining power. The mismatch framing gives the gender-revolution literature a specific mechanism — a stalled renegotiation between the sexes — rather than a general reference to changing norms.
entries.title: The Rise of Female Autonomy and the Decline of Fertility: The Role of Mismatch

entries.keyArgument:
Onofri, Berniell, Fernández and Menduiña decompose Latin America's fertility decline between 2000 and 2022 and find it is driven mainly by within-group reductions — fertility falling for a given age and education level — rather than by the population shifting toward groups (older, more educated) that already had fewer children. The reduction is concentrated among younger and less-educated women, which cuts against a simple story of rising education mechanically lowering the aggregate rate.

Comparing women born in the mid-1950s to those born in the mid-1970s, they show lower completed fertility reflects both delayed childbearing and a real reduction in the average number of children per woman who does have children, not a rise in childlessness. This gives the region's decline a similar shape to the Geruso-Spears finding for the Indian context already in this corpus: parity progression, not childlessness, doing most of the work.
entries.title: Understanding Latin America's Fertility Decline: Age, Education, and Cohort Dynamics

entries.keyArgument:
A brief but sharp empirical statement of the desired/achieved fertility gap, set in the most extreme low-fertility context in Europe: Italy, at a total fertility rate of 1.18 in 2024 and the continent's highest mean age at first birth, 31.8 years, in 2023.

The authors find that more than half of Italian men and women reach the end of their reproductive years wishing they had had more children than they did — unmet fertility desire on a scale that makes it a central, not marginal, feature of the Italian case. Read alongside the corpus's other unrealized-fertility entries, Italy stands as the sharpest test case: if desire itself is falling as fast as some theories propose, an unmet-desire gap this large is harder to explain than one where desire and constraint both matter.
entries.title: Unmet Fertility Desires: Evidence from a Lowest-Low Fertility Context

entries.keyArgument:
Drawing on the Global Survey of Working Arrangements and the U.S. Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes, the authors find that both realized fertility (2021 to early 2025) and planned future fertility are higher among adults who work from home at least one day a week — and higher still among couples where both partners do. Estimated lifetime fertility is 0.32 children per woman greater when both partners work from home versus when neither does.

The mechanism proposed is straightforward: flexibility in when, where and how work happens lowers the practical cost of combining child-rearing with employment, a structural condition distinct from income, price, policy or ideation. Because WFH adoption rates vary enormously across countries, the authors note the implications for aggregate national fertility differ accordingly — the effect is real but its macro impact depends on how much remote work a given labor market actually allows.
entries.publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research / EBRD / CESifo
entries.title: Work from Home and Fertility

entries.keyArgument:
Rotkirch takes the concept of reproductive cues from life history theory in evolutionary biology and applies it to the contemporary childbearing landscape. Cues are environmental signals for when it is a good time to have and raise offspring, and, she stresses, crucially also for when it appears to be a very bad idea.

The argument is that the bodies and minds of young women have evolved to be attuned to the examples of their peers, the support available from kin and community, and the status and encouragement or discouragement coming from the broader environment. Bodily, social, institutional and technological cues together shape the timing of parenthood.

The mismatch she identifies is that economic, technological and institutional incentives increasingly favour ever later childbearing while biological fertility does not, producing lower birth rates and involuntary childlessness. This is the paper to read against your own work on cue depletion.
entries.title: “Think about it all the time”. Reproductive cues in a late and low fertility setting
